description:
We are Cosmic Chaos Crew, six 3rd year Electronics and Communication engineering students from St. Joseph's College of Engineering , Chennai. 

We share an interest in space technology, data and building practical tools. Space Apps 2026 let us work with real NASA satellite data, and together we built and deployed a live web app that uses it.
summary:
FireHarmonize is a live web dashboard that harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections so that a fire seen by both sensors is counted once, not twice. The two instruments differ in resolution (about 1 km vs 375 m), confidence scales and overpass times, so simply combining their data double-counts fires and distorts fire statistics and trends.

Our backend pulls near-real-time data from the NASA FIRMS API every hour, converts both sensors into one format, flags duplicates and low-confidence detections, and pairs MODIS and VIIRS detections within 2 km and 180 minutes using a weighted match score. Every detection is labelled matched, MODIS-only or VIIRS-only and grouped into harmonized fire events, shown on an interactive map with adjustable matching controls, trends and a searchable data explorer.

It runs today on live data for Punjab & Haryana and South India. On real data we also found that MODIS Aqua now passes over India about 2 hours after VIIRS because of orbit drift, which explains why so few detections can be matched, and the dashboard measures and shows this gap.
details:
What it does:

FireHarmonize is a live web dashboard that combines active-fire detections from NASA's two fire-sensing instruments, MODIS (Terra and Aqua satellites, about 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, 375 m pixels), so that a fire seen by both sensors is counted once instead of twice.

How it works:

1. Every hour the backend downloads the last 3 days of MODIS_NRT and VIIRS_NOAA21_NRT detections from the NASA FIRMS API for each region (Punjab & Haryana, and South India).

2. Both sensors are converted into one common format. VIIRS confidence (low/nominal/high) is mapped to heuristic scores of 25/60/90 so it can be compared with MODIS's 0-100 scale.

3. Repeated detections (within 0.2 km and 60 seconds) and detections below confidence 30 are flagged and kept out of matching.

4. Each MODIS detection is paired with at most one VIIRS detection within 2 km and 180 minutes. Candidate pairs are ranked by a match score (50% distance, 30% time, 20% confidence) and accepted greedily, best first.

5. Every detection is labelled matched, MODIS-only or VIIRS-only and grouped into harmonized fire events.

The dashboard shows the results in six views: Overview, Fire Map on satellite imagery, Harmonization (sliders to change the rules and re-run matching), Historical Trends, Data Explorer and Methodology. It works on phones.

Results on live data:

For 12-13 November 2026, Punjab & Haryana had 722 raw detections (323 MODIS, 399 VIIRS); 33 were flagged and 11 MODIS-VIIRS pairs were matched, giving 678 harmonized events. South India had 1,076 raw detections, 166 flagged and 9 pairs, giving 901 events.

Benefits and intended impact:

Counting each fire once gives more accurate fire totals and trends for researchers, agencies and anyone monitoring crop-residue burning and wildfires. The app shows exactly how each detection was treated, so the results can be checked rather than taken on trust.

What makes it creative:

Our first run on real data found zero matches. Instead of assuming a bug, we measured each satellite's pass time from the detections themselves and found that MODIS Aqua, launched in 2002, now passes over India about 2 hours 12 minutes after VIIRS NOAA-21 because its orbit has drifted. The dashboard measures this gap from live data and explains it on screen, and the matching window was adapted to it.

Factors we considered:

Accuracy (one-to-one matching, flags for low-confidence and repeat detections), transparency (every rule and weight is shown and adjustable), reliability (hourly caching per region, the last good copy kept if NASA is unreachable, clearly labelled demo data as a last resort), security (the NASA API key stays on the server), cost (free hosting and free data) and honesty about limits: this is a prototype method, not an official NASA algorithm, and a matched pair is strong evidence of one fire, not proof.

Tools and languages:

Python (FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn BallTree for fast distance search), TypeScript and React 18 (Vite, Tailwind, Leaflet, Recharts), NASA FIRMS API, Esri ArcGIS basemaps. Hosted on Render (backend) and Vercel (frontend). 26 automated tests. No special hardware.

Use of AI tools:

Our team chose the challenge, the regions and the harmonization approach, set the requirements, obtained the NASA FIRMS API access, deployed the system, and tested every feature on live NASA data. We used AI assistants (Claude by Anthropic and ChatGPT by OpenAI) as tools to speed up coding, debugging, documentation and slide design. When our first live run returned zero matches, we investigated the real detections, identified MODIS Aqua's overpass drift and decided how the matching should adapt. All fire data comes directly from NASA FIRMS; none of it is AI-generated.

Live dashboard: https://fire-harmonize.vercel.app
